title: Exact random-order ratio of Best-Fit bin packing
short_statement: In online bin packing under uniformly random arrival order, determine the exact asymptotic performance ratio of the classical Best-Fit algorithm.
background: Bin packing is one of the canonical models of resource allocation: items of different sizes must be assigned to the minimum number of unit-capacity bins. The online version models packing, memory allocation, scheduling, and admission decisions when future jobs are unknown. Worst-case online bin packing is deliberately pessimistic; adversarial order lets an input designer reveal items in a sequence that is much worse than a typical shuffled instance. Kenyon's random-order model keeps the multiset adversarial but randomizes the arrival order, creating a clean beyond-worst-case benchmark. Best-Fit is especially important because it is simple, deterministic, and used in practice. The random-order analysis asks whether the empirical robustness of Best-Fit has a theorem-level explanation. The problem is also technically attractive: it mixes online irrevocability, random permutations, and packing structure. The main difficulty is that Best-Fit creates state-dependent residual capacities; early random fluctuations determine which gaps remain for later items, and these dependencies are hard to summarize by a small set of statistics.
full_statement: Let $I=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}$ be a multiset of item sizes in $(0,1]$. A uniformly random permutation of $I$ is revealed online. The algorithm sees each item size on arrival and must immediately and irrevocably place it into an open unit-capacity bin or open a new bin. The Best-Fit algorithm places an arriving item into a feasible open bin that leaves the smallest remaining capacity after insertion, opening a new bin only when no open bin can fit the item. Let $BF(\pi(I))$ be the number of bins used by Best-Fit on random order $\pi$, and let $OPT(I)$ be the minimum number of bins in an offline packing of $I$. The random-order ratio of Best-Fit is the least $\rho$ such that $\mathbb E_{\pi}[BF(\pi(I))]\le \rho\,OPT(I)+o(OPT(I))$ for all item multisets $I$. Determine this constant $\rho$. Kenyon historically conjectured a value near $1.15$; the published lower bound $1.15582656$ now rules out $1.15$ as an exact upper bound. The open problem is not to design a better algorithm, but to characterize the exact worst-case random-order behavior of one fixed, widely used heuristic. A complete solution would either prove a matching upper and lower bound, or identify the right extremal family showing that the conjectured value is wrong.
known_results: Kenyon's SODA 1996 work established an upper bound of $1.5$ and a lower bound of $1.08$ for the random-order ratio of Best-Fit, and conjectured a value around $1.15$. Albers, Khan, and Ladewig improved the special case in which every item has size larger than $1/3$, giving a $1.25$ upper bound and a $1.1$ lower bound for that restricted regime. Ayyadevara, Dabas, Khan, and Sreenivas settled the iid stochastic model with a $(1+\varepsilon)$-competitive meta-algorithm and made progress on random-order special cases, including items in $(1/4,1/2]$. Hebbar, Khan, and Sreenivas then gave the first general improvement over the $3/2$ barrier, proving an upper bound $1.5-\varepsilon$ for a fixed positive constant $\varepsilon$, and improved the lower bound to $1.144$, close to Kenyon's conjectured value. The exact constant remains open: the best known upper bound is still far from the lower bound, and no known structural theorem identifies the extremal random-order instances. Epstein and Levin (WADS 2025), Theorem 10, improve the asymptotic lower bound to $1.15582656$. Their separate absolute lower bound $1.5$ (Proposition 11) is not an asymptotic bound.

progress.summary: The asymptotic ratio lies between $1.15582656$ (Epstein-Levin 2025) and $1.5-\varepsilon$ for a fixed positive constant (Hebbar-Khan-Sreenivas 2024). Its exact value remains open.

links.title: Epstein and Levin, WADS 2025 lower bounds

counterexample_rationale: Lower bounds are explicit adversarial multisets analyzed under random permutation. Automated search can look for finite item-size patterns whose Best-Fit random-order expectation exceeds known lower bounds.
alphaevolve_rationale: A search loop can generate candidate multisets, estimate Best-Fit behavior exactly or by simulation, and optimize lower-bound constructions. It can also search for state summaries suggesting sharper upper-bound potentials.

literature.synthesis: The literature has progressed by separating item-size regimes. Kenyon gave the baseline random-order framework and the original $1.5$ upper bound. Later work improved special intervals such as items larger than $1/3$ or in $(1/4,1/2]$, where the packing structure is much more constrained. Hebbar, Khan, and Sreenivas showed that the full problem is not stuck at $3/2$, but their improvement is deliberately small and technical. Epstein and Levin's 2025 lower bound exceeds $1.15$; the extremal asymptotic ratio remains undetermined. The remaining gap is a constant-factor structural gap for one fixed algorithm. Any upper-bound proof must control the distribution of residual bin capacities created by Best-Fit under a random permutation for arbitrary item multisets; any lower-bound proof must turn a finite pattern into an asymptotic family and rigorously compute its expected bin count.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: For lower bounds, search over rational item sizes with repeated types, compute or tightly estimate Best-Fit's expected number of bins under random order, and compare to an exact offline optimum. For upper bounds, try potential functions over residual-capacity intervals, martingale concentration over random permutations, or reductions to a finite set of troublesome size classes.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed lower bound must specify an infinite family of item multisets, prove the offline optimum asymptotically, and prove the expected Best-Fit bin count under random order. A claimed upper bound must hold for every multiset, not only iid inputs or fixed size classes. Simulation can suggest candidates but cannot by itself certify a new ratio. A referee should check whether all additive $o(OPT)$ terms are controlled, whether ties in Best-Fit are handled consistently or shown irrelevant, and whether the proof uses uniform random permutation rather than iid sampling with replacement.

where_posed.text: The conjecture and remaining gap are discussed in Hebbar, Khan, Sreenivas, 'Bin Packing under Random-Order: Breaking the Barrier of 3/2', SODA 2024.
